en: Salutations to the venerable gurus.
May there be no obstacles.
The foundational verse of the palace.
{An Explanation of Six Verses} ||
From the root, the lotus that is the dwelling place of Kuṇḍalinī, there arises a swan-like sound; Śiva resides within the navel like a firefly with a momentary flash of light.
Above that, at a distance of one span (vitasti), the heart-lotus is situated at four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula).
The flame of the blazing fire, drenched by clouds, spreads over the morning sun. || 1 ||
O Blessed Lord, seated upon the lotus-throne, you are the Master of the twenty-four principles;
marked by the moon and sun— the light of the two syllables *ka* and *ṇa*— along with the thumb and little finger,
you are the Supreme Person accompanied by Lakṣmī, together with the six principles of the Vedānta.
One should cause [the practitioner] to remember that on the tongue, at a distance of four finger-breadths, there is a portion of poison marked by the measure.

Resplendent like a streak of lightning, with the cremation ground as its playground and Māyā as its companion, the syllable *Hāṃ* is situated there between the eyebrows; it consists of two fingers' breadth, resembling a lamp-flame,
joined by the expansion of the half-measure (*mātrā*) and the dot (*bindu*), and it possesses the arms of knowledge.
Furthermore, there is a half-moon marked with blood, and one marked with a single foot of Dhātṛ. || 3 ||
At the tip of the plowshare (phāla), the light previously described is known as the Rodhikalā, measuring one-eighth of a mātrā;
the staff (daṇḍa) is sixteen parts, resembling a jewel, located behind the aperture of Brahmā.
Within that staff is this sprout-like light, appearing from half of its own measure.
From the middle of the two creeper-like eyebrows, having accepted three principles (tattvas) measured by nine finger-breadths; || 4 ||
The Lord Īśasada himself occupies four *padas* beginning with Bindvardha; above that, in a single *aṅgula-pada*, is Śakti, who consists of a portion of Kalā and Aṃśa.
There are three voids consisting of a portion of Kalā, and above those, Vyāpinī occupies three *aṅgulas*.
Afterwards, [the next part] consists of twice that number of divisions, having the form of a trident and endowed with a pair of dots. || 5 ||
O Lord, that certain power called Unmanā, which consists of fifty-six parts— leaving a remainder of two after ten pairs of rows of fifty-six—
is subtle-bodied, extends for four finger-breadths, and reaches as far as the limit of the attachment to bonds;
she, the Unmanā, reigns supreme within those four finger-breadths.
When the fourfold power was destroyed, Śiva, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns at the end of an aeon, was struck down.
[The Explanation of the Six Verses on the Palace]
O Lord of the Gaṇas, according to my own understanding and by a mere fragment of Your grace,
I now write this brief commentary on the *Śrīmatprāsāda* in six verses.

Now, since the *hauṃ* syllable— which constitutes the five-syllable seed-mantra (*bīja*) expressive of Paramaśiva— is described in many ways within the Śaiva scriptures through its divisions into three, five, eight, nine, twelve, sixteen,
and other kalās, herein [we consider] the twelve kalās of the Prāsāda mantra according to their metrical measures (*mātrā*).

Having understood the pervasion of the *kalā* (power) within the *kṛtya* (action) by means of the excellent power (*suśakti*) in the path of the empty fingers known as the *kāraṇākhyāna-sthāna*, who indeed would not be liberated? Thus, having described [this] primarily, the Teacher, intending to define the twelve-fold temple (*prāsāda*) with six verses, first [describes] the origin of the letter *ha*.

The pervasion of the locations is stated by half a verse: "From the root, the abode of the residence of Kuṇḍalinī, Śiva remains as far as the navel, resembling a sprout with a momentary flash of light, having a voice as gentle as a swan.
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: from the root, which is the abode of the residence of Kuṇḍalinī, [he who has] a voice as gentle as a swan.
"Śiva, resembling a momentary flash of light, dwells within the navel"—this is the meaning.

From the abode that is the dwelling place of Kuṇḍalinī—that is, from the residence or house of Māyā purified by Kuṇḍalinī—he has arisen from the root-lotus, that is, from the *mūlādhāra* lotus; this is the ellipsis. He possesses the sound of a peacock (*mayūra-rāja-svanaḥ*).

The sound of *haṃsa*; resembling a flash of lightning or a sprout, equal to the burgeoning of a thunderbolt; consisting merely of the letter *ha*—devoid of vowel and possessing only the form of a consonant—the syllable *haṃ* alone is Śiva, the seed of Śiva. It abides, existing as far as the navel, reaching up to the lotus of the navel. Below it is the Kuṇḍalinī power, which is Māyā.

The stability of the world is such that its effect consists of *nāda* and *bindu*, following the course of karma; this is established by the statement in the *Śataratnasaṃgraha*: "Even the seed of Śiva is produced from the power of Kuṇḍalinī.
By those whose minds are concentrated on the ear-cavities covered with cotton and the like, it resounds like the cry of a swan (*haṃsa*).
Because the subtle resonance (*sūkṣmanāda*) is being heard, its quality of being free from impurity (*malālasvanatva*) is established.

By stating the distinction between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), its nature as Śiva is established. Since only the consonant (*vyañjana*) is to be discussed here—due to its connection with the *medhākalā* which will be explained further on—the usage *ha-mātra* (the mere *ha*) and *mātra* [is employed].
It has been established. The reading "hammātraśśivaḥ" is easily understood. For it is stated that "there is no cognition of a person whatsoever apart from sound";

thus, because [Śiva] is the illuminator by virtue of being the means of cognition, his nature as light is proven, and consequently, his state of possessing the brilliance of lightning is established. As for the restriction of the location "within those two," it applies to one who is devoid of the digit of intelligence (medhā-kalā).
Likewise, the rule regarding the location is that it extends as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) for one who is accompanied [by the breath]; this is the intended meaning.

Now, regarding the measure of the digit (kalā) of Medhā, he describes the principles (tattvas) of the locations named Kānti, Kāraṇeśvara, and Sthānāṅgula by means of three quarters of a verse: "Above that, on a foot [of the body] extending one span (vitasti), the heart-lotus is four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula);
above that, the blooming fire and Śiva pervade it, drenched by Medhā. [Therein reside] the principles (tattvas) seated upon the lotus-throne."
"The Blessed One said, 'This is not [the case] for twenty-four. Herein, the construction of the words is as follows:

above that, when the foot has leaped a span (vitasti), the heart-lotus is four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) [above]; above that, Medhā, whose splendor is like the flame of a blazing fire, pervades the space reached by the leap."

The Lord Nātha, seated upon a lotus throne, is the master of the twenty-four principles (tattvas). His seat is the navel-lotus; above that, at a distance of two spans (dvitastī)—that is, exceeding twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas)—is the location of the heart-lotus (hṛtkaja), which measures four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) in size. Above that...
Above that, the *plutā* (protracted) vowel is three measures (*trimātrā*), possessing the radiance of a blossoming flame of fire and resembling a blazing fire;

it presides over the four primary principles (*catuḥ-prakṛti-tattvānām*) and the twenty-four principles (*caturviṃśati-tattvānām*). Seated upon a lotus throne is the Lord Brahmā, the Master (*nātha*) and Sovereign of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*). Starting from the navel-lotus, he is accompanied by Medhā.
The meaning is that the letter *ha* pervades as far as the heart-lotus.
[Now the second verse:]
With the second and third words, he defines the aesthetic essence (*rasakalā*):

"The Lord (*nātha*), the Supreme Person (*pumān*) who has Lakṣmī as his companion, who is marked by two measures (*dvimātrā*) and possesses the six principles (*ṣaṭkatattva*) of the end of the Vedas (*śrutyanta*), [and who is] the moon and the sun in the neck (*kaṇṭha*) and the ring-finger (*iṣṭāṅgulika*). Here, the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) is to be supplied.

The meaning, however, is as follows: starting from the heart-lotus at a distance of eight finger-breadths (aṣṭāṅgula) and extending to the throat—that is, in the region up to the throat—the letter *ū* is marked with two measures (*dvimātrāṅkita*), being endowed with two measures; it is the light of the moon and the sun, like the moon-gem (*candrakānta*) and the sun-gem (*tapanakānta*), and it is the *śruti* of the end of the *śruti*.
The right ear is *ta*, and its end is the left ear; its corresponding letter is *ū*.

This [syllable] is joined with the six principles (*tattva*) known as Kalā, Vidya, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, and Puruṣa—being endowed with these six principles and accompanied by Lakṣmī because she causes his persistence, the Person named Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, is the agent who serves as the cause of protection.

Regarding the term *kāraṇeśvara*: the sense is that it pervades the letter *ū* from the heart-lotus up to the end of the throat. Now, he describes the "poison-portion" (*viṣakalā*) by means of the fourth quarter of the second verse and the first quarter of the third verse.
On the tongue, which measures four finger-breadths, one should cause [the disciple] to remember the measure marked by a sixteenth part of poison.
"Like a streak of lightning, beautiful, the world, the cremation ground, with Māyā as his companion, Hara"— the construction of the words here is as follows: on the tongue four finger-breadths long,
one should cause [the practitioner] to remember the portion of poison marked by the measures, beautiful like a streak of lightning, the world, the cremation ground, accompanied by Māyā, and Hara.

The meaning, however, is as follows: on the tongue, which measures four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula), starting from the root of the throat and extending to the root of the tongue, there is a marked measure of one mātrā;
she whose radiance is like the luster of a garland of lightning—that is, whose splendor is like that of a mass of streaks of lightning—is thus described.

The syllable *makāra* is a portion of poison (*viṣakalā*). "The world is a cremation ground" (*jagat pitṛvanam*) means that the worlds—the universes—are a cremation ground (*pitṛvana*), so called because Rudra performs the function of destruction (*saṃhāra*). In the reading *jagat pitryam*, it means the world has the nature of the ancestors (*pitṛsvarūpa*) and is accompanied by Māyā; [it belongs] to Māyā.

The phrase "the companion and collaborator of Mohinī" means that by the expression "having Māyā as his companion," it should be understood that the single principle of Māyā-tattva is stated here as a constituent element within the portion of poison. "One should remember Hara" means one should meditate upon Rudra;
the meaning is that one should contemplate the agent of action (karmakāra) starting from the root of the throat up to the root of the tongue.
The state of being.
[Now, the third verse:]
With the second and third quarters, he defines the *bindu-kalā*.

In that regard, one should meditate on the Vidyā, presided over by her arms, as being situated between the eyebrows at a distance of two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgulika), rivaling a lamp-flame in its brilliance, joined with half a *mātrā*, combined with the two principles (*dvitatva*), and marked by a dot (*bindu*). The remainder [of the visualization] is as follows:
having remained there, [one should contemplate] from the root of the tongue up to the end of the space between the eyebrows, measuring two finger-breadths.
Between the eyebrows, at the limit of the space between them, is a lamp-flame rivaling [the sun];

it is joined with half a mātrā consisting of only a surrounding circle, measuring half a mātrā, the two principles (tattva) united, together with the Lord (Īśvara) in Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā), the Bindu, and the digit of the Bindu (bindukalā) held by the arms of Knowledge.

The meaning is that one should meditate upon it as presided over by Maheśvara. The intention is that one should meditate on the digit of the Bindu (bindukalā) starting from the root of the palate up to the middle of the eyebrows.
Now, by the fourth quarter of the third verse, he describes the digit of the half-moon.
"The half-bindu, moreover, beautiful as a half-moon, marked by a single mātrā"—
the construction of the words is: "one should contemplate the half-bindu,
beautiful as a half-moon, marked by a single mātrā, and having a movement resembling a half-moon."

This *pada* should be known as effective for spreading radiance (*kānti*). "Marked by a single *mātrā*" means marked by one *mātrā*, that is, one part of a foot; a single part of a foot is a fourth part.
Thus, it is marked or characterized by that, meaning it is endowed with a quarter-measure (*pādamātra*). "Half a *bindu*"—

The meaning is that one should meditate upon the digit (kalā) of the half-moon. It should be understood that the four digits beginning with the half-moon and ending with the resonance (nāda)— along with their locations, finger-measures (aṅgula), principles (tattva), and presiding deities— are not described here separately, as they will be explained later on.
The meaning is that above the *bindu-kalā* there is the *ardhacandra-kalā*, which is called Bhavānī.

Now, with the first quarter of the fourth verse, he defines the *nirodhikalā*: "The *nirodhikalā* is said to have the luster previously mentioned, and to consist of one-eighth of a *mātrā*. The meaning is that its luster is as previously described—that is, a lunar radiance—and it consists of one-eighth of a *mātrā*, which is one-eighth of a single *mātrā*.

The time for one-eighth part is one part. This is what is meant: the time for the utterance of the letter *ma* is half a *kalā*; the time for the utterance of the *bindu* is half the time of the utterance of the *bindu*; [and] the time of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

At the time of the half-moon, the cessation of the *kalā* should be known as "time" (*kāla*). The *kalā* that obstructs and the *kalā* that is obstructed are remembered as "contemplated" (*cintita*); this is the meaning. In this [state], the expansion (*prastāra*) takes the form of a triangle.
Now, by means of the second and third quarters of the fourth verse, he describes the *nādāntakalā* (the digit at the end of sound):

"The staff (*daṇḍa*) is sixteen parts, resembling a jewel, located behind in the cavity of Brahman; at the end of the staff, there is light comparable to a flash of lightning or a sprout, occupying half a part."

The word-order is as follows: "The staff (daṇḍa), resembling a jewel, consists of sixteen parts; behind it, within the aperture of Brahmā, there is the light of the staff situated inside, possessing the radiance of a flash of lightning from half a part.
The term *ṣoḍaśakāṃśakaḥ* means that it possesses a single portion consisting of sixteen parts by measure (*mātrā*). It is endowed with such a measure.

Resembling a jewel, with a luster equal to a ruby; the staff (daṇḍa) is the expansion in the form of a staff of the art of sound (nādakalā). Thus, after the art of sound, above it, in the cavity of Brahmā—that is, in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra)—it extends up to that limit by half-parts of each respective sound.

With a measure of one part out of thirty-two, its light rivals the sprout of lightning; it possesses a splendor like a flash of lightning. The remainder is that the *kalā* (digit) pervades from the end of the *daṇḍa* to the end of the *nāda*. Furthermore, they describe its arrangement (*prastāra*) as having the form of a plowshare (*halākṛti*), with a *bindu* on each of the two sides of the *nāda*.
The arrangement [of the letters] for *nādānta* on the right side is like a consonant (*hal*) joined with the *bindu*. Now,
by means of the fourth quarter of the fourth verse and the first quarter of the fifth verse,

there is the measurement in finger-breadths (*aṅgula-tattva*) of the previously mentioned digits (*kalā*) of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the obstructing one (*nirodhinī*), resonance (*nāda*), and the end of resonance (*nādānta*).

Regarding the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*), [the text] says: "From the middle of the two creeper-like eyebrows, at a distance of one *javenāṅgula*, having accepted the three principles (*tattva*) beginning with half of the *bindu* of the four-footed [mantra], the Blessed Lord himself is the eternal place of Īśa. That is to say, from the middle of the two creeper-like eyebrows, at a distance of one *bhavāṅgula*, having accepted the three principles beginning with half of the *bindu* of the fourfold [set].

The syntactical construction of the words is: "The Blessed One himself is the Lord of all places. Starting from the point of the *bindu* (the dot) in the middle region, that is, from between the two creeper-like eyebrows (*bhrūlatā*), at a distance measured by eleven *bhava*-fingers—here the word *bhava* denotes Rudra, as there are eleven Rudras—at this location measuring eleven fingers, [is the place].

Here too, the number eleven is accepted. Having accepted—that is, having acknowledged—the three principles (tattvas) consisting of the four parts beginning with *bindvardha*, the four digits (kalās) beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and the four digits beginning with the half-moon up to the end of sound (*nādānta*) ending with *nirodhinī*; and having accepted the triad of principles consisting of Sādākhya, Śakti, and Śiva, the Blessed One [proceeds].

The meaning is that the Lord of Causes (Kāraṇeśvara) himself is present there with his own region. According to the statement, "from the middle of the eyebrows to the end of the Brahma-randhra is two fingers minus one quarter," and considering that the measurement from the location of the Bindu to the end of the Brahma-randhra is eleven finger-breadths (aṅgulas), [this applies] to the Ardhacandra-kalā.

The meaning is that the space for the four *kalās* is eleven finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*), being three finger-breadths less than half [of the total height] above the midpoint of the eyebrows. Now, regarding the distinction of the measurement in finger-breadths: in the human proportion of ninety-six finger-breadths, there are forty-eight finger-breadths from the feet up to the *mūlādhāra*.

Without abandoning the forty-eight finger-breadths from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*, [one perceives] sound (*ghoṣa*) extending for twelve finger-breadths from the *mūlādhāra* to the navel within those forty-eight finger-breadths from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*.

The place beginning from the navel and ending at the heart-lotus is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long; it is accompanied by Ghoṣa and is the place of the Medhā-kalā. The place beginning from the heart-lotus and ending at the throat-base is eight finger-breadths long; it is accompanied by Ghoṣa and Medhā and is the place of the Rasa-kalā. [The place] beginning from the throat-base and ending at the root of the tongue is four finger-breadths long.

The place of Ghoṣā, Medhā, Rasa, and Kalā, together with the portion of poison, is located from the root of the tongue up to the middle of the eyebrows; it is two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent. From the place of the Bindu to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is ten finger-breadths, comprising the Ardhacandra, Nirodhinī, Nāda, and Nādānta.

This should be known as the locus of the *kalās*. The sound of the *haṃsa*, produced by the power of Kuṇḍalinī situated at the *mūlādhāra*—the letter *ha*, which is the seed-syllable of Śiva—travels through the path of the *suṣumṇā*. Modified by its union with the *kalās* such as *medhā* and the rest, it is heard again as *nāda* near the *brahmarandhra*; there itself, it reaches the state of *nādānta*.
It should be understood that he does not abide in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Now, with the second quarter of the fifth verse, he describes the Śakti-kalā: "Above that, at a distance of one finger-breadth, is the Śakti-kalā, which consists of a portion of a portion. The construction of the words is as follows: "Now, above that, at a distance of one finger-breadth, is the Śakti consisting of a portion of a portion."

The meaning of "atha" (now) is as follows: immediately after the determination of the end of the sound (*nāda*), therefore, above the *brahma-śilā*, in each successive place measured by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*),

one should contemplate the Power (*śakti*)— the remainder being that she is endowed with measure (*mātrā*) and joined with the portion of the digit (*kalā-aṃśikā*), which consists of sixty-four parts.

On its left side, there is the form of a *hal* (plow) joined with a *bindu*, possessing a beautiful radiance like a hundred suns; this is to be known as the unstruck (*anāhata*) Śiva, the Lord of Causes, belonging to the quartet of digits beginning with *Śakti*. Now, by the second half of the fifth verse, [it describes] that which moves within the void situated in the midst of the nine digits beginning with *Medhā* and ending with *Śakti*.
He describes the pervasive power (*vyāpinī-kalā*): "The voids [are formed] from a third of the three powers;
above that, three finger-breadths, with a portion double that, endowed with a pair of dots, in the form of a trident—this is the *vyāpinī*. The meaning is as follows:

from a third of the three powers—the division of the three powers beginning with *medhā* (wisdom)—there are the voids, which are the three voids: *medhā*, *rasa* (flavor), and... [the rest of the sentence continues].

At the conclusion of the objects (*viṣaya*), the first void (*śūnya*) ceases along with the Bindu, Ardhacandra, and Nirodhinī; this is to be known as the second void. At the conclusion of the Kalās—Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, and Kalā—the third void is to be known.
Among the Kalās known as Medhā and the rest, up to Ārka, there are groups of three by three; the void occurs at their cessation.

According to the statement, "In the realm of form, there is a void for each successive reduction; beyond that void, I join the Śaiva [principle]," following the description of the *śaktikalā*, above that— in a space measuring three fingers' breadth, two fingers above the one-finger [space] leading upward from the *brahmarandhra*— there are portions double that size.

Of that previously mentioned number sixty-four, the double is one hundred and twenty-eight; thus, the form of the trident (śūla) consists of two dots (bindu) possessing a measure equal to a single part of those one hundred and twenty-eight parts. It is accompanied by two dots.
Some say that from the expansion of the portion of the trident, together with the right-pointing bindu, the form of the trident arises.

The remainder is that the pervasive *vyāpinī* is to be meditated upon as the pervasive *kalā*. Its radiance is like that of a thousand suns; it should be known that the unstruck (*anāhata*) Śiva himself is the agent.
Now, with the first half of six verses, he defines *samanā* as having an equal number of digits (*kalā*).

"Endowed with six, consisting of fifty, ten, and two remaining parts, with subtle limbs, within four fingers, *samanā* extends up to the limit of the connection with the bonds (*pāśa*). Now, within those four fingers, endowed with six...

The construction of the words is as follows: "Samanā" is that which consists of fifty-four parts—remaining after subtracting ten pairs from fifty—and is subtle-limbed, with its limit being the connection to the *pāśa*. As for the meaning:
next, within the *vyāpinī*, at a distance of four finger-breadths above the *brahmarandhra* and four finger-breadths further upward...
In the space of four finger-breadths (aṅgula), there are fifty lines (pañcāśat-paṅkti) combined with six;
taking two pairs of ten (daśaka-dvandva-śa-tad-dvaya), that is, twenty, and adding them together, one part out of two hundred and fifty-six is the measure [of each line].
Therefore, she is "fine-limbed" (sūkṣmāṅgī), meaning her form can be discerned by a time that is not excessively subtle.

The limit of the attachment to bonds (*pāśānuṣaṅga*) extends to the full extent of the involvement with bonds, up to the level of *Samanā*. According to the statement, "Beyond [this] is Paraśiva," it follows that the *kalā* of *Samanā* is to be meditated upon as the end of the web of bonds. As long as the activity of the mind (*manas*) persists, so long does the attachment to bonds continue; when the operation of the mind is stilled, then...
The attainment of the state: as it is said in the *Śataratnasaṃgraha*:
"When the mind, having found its mark in the ultimate reality, becomes absorbed therein, then all discursive cognition undergoes destruction."
In the Sūta Saṃhitā as well:
"O bulls among the gods, when the activity of the mind has ceased,
one knows its absence through self-luminosity, even during deep sleep."
In the *Siddhāntadīpikā* as well, it is said:
"Relying upon existence within non-existence, one should bring about existence without support;
having made the mind mindless, one should not contemplate anything at all."
There are no senses, nor vital breath, nor mind, nor intellect, nor desire;
I am not this, nor is this in me, through the dissolution of the mind.
Through the exhaustion of the mind, there is the supreme pervasion—this is the truth, O Mother of the Gaṇas.
And so it is said. Let us return to the subject at hand: together with the *manas*, she is *samanā*; such is the meaning of the word *samanā*.
Her expansion (*prastāra*) consists of six [units], equal to ten million suns, situated between two dots (*bindu*) like the letter *ṭa*.
Now, with the second half of the sixth verse, there is a description of the *unmanā* state, as well as [the mention] of Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, Unmanā, and the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśa*).
That Śakti, known as *unmanā*, shines forth within four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) of the Lord;
she possesses the splendor of ten million suns at the end of an aeon (*kalpārka-koṭi-dyuti*), and she is the beloved speech (*iṣṭokti*) of the fourfold [reality] of Śiva.

Such is the word-by-word construction (*padayojanā*). Within the four-finger space (*caturaṅgula*), there shines a certain power (*śakti*) called Unmanā, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns at the end of an aeon; she triumphs as the supreme power within the fourfold group of powers, while Śiva, having been absorbed by her, also triumphs. As for the meaning: within the measure of four fingers located above the Brahma-aperture (*brahmarandhra*), extending eight fingers upward, [reside] the powers and so forth.
According to the statement, "above the *vilas* [are] three, four, and four finger-breadths," the meaning is "in the uppermost four-finger-breadth space.

She possesses the splendor of ten million suns at the end of an eon (*kalpa*), a light like ten million suns blazing at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*). She is thus described as one whose mind has reached the state called *unmanā*;
she whose name is *unmanā*—the mental activity—is so called. *Unmanā* is her name. Her mental function is [thus characterized].

The supreme power of the Lord Paramaśiva, that certain extraordinary and renowned *parāśakti* which bestows peace, reigns as something transcendent. Now, since the mind, the self-principle (*ātmatattva*), and the twenty-four principles have been heard [in scripture], there are the seven *vidyā*-principles and the five *śiva*-principles, namely: will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

If it is asked how the state of *unmanā* (the transcendent mind) belongs to the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), which exists beyond both power (*śakti*) and primordial power (*ādi-śakti*), the answer is as follows:
the principle of Īśvara is the effect of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*);

the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddha-vidyā-tattva*) is the effect of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); and the principle of Śakti is the effect of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Thus, the principle of Īśvara...

The principle of *pravṛtti* (activity) functions for the impulsion of the principle of *rāga* (attachment); the principle of *vidyā* functions for the impulsion of the principle of *śuddhavidyā*; and the principle of *kāla* (time) functions for the impulsion of the principle of *śakti*. Furthermore, through the principle of *rāga*, the principle of *manas* (mind) functions; through the principle of *aśuddhavidyā*, the principle of *buddhi* (intellect) functions; and through the principle of *kāla*, the principle of *ahaṃkāra* (ego) functions.

"Activity" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the operation of the principles of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the self (*ātma-tattva*); this is the meaning of all the scriptures (*sarvāgama*). Therefore, all the principles (*tattvas*) that constitute the effects of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) are established as being of the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) within the mind (*manas*). Regarding this, there is a supporting statement from the *Siddhāntarahasyasāra*: [Insert Sanskrit verse here] (Note: The specific Sanskrit verse from the *Siddhāntarahasyasāra* was not provided in the source text, so it is indicated by a placeholder.)

"Just as the mind (manas) is the instrument that causes the senses to engage with their objects, moving swiftly and always forming intentions, and whose nature is desire (*icchā*)— the source of birth [and bondage]— therefore, when the principle of the mind, whose essence is the power of desire, is stilled, it is logical that the powers of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) are likewise stilled."

If it is asked from where will desire (*icchā*), power (*śakti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), and peace (*śānti*) arise, it is said: The emergence of the Primordial Power (*ādi-śakti*) is from a thousandth part of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*). The emergence of the Power of Desire (*icchā-śakti*) is from a thousandth part of the Primordial Power. [From a thousandth part of the Power of Desire...]

Because of the statement, "The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) arises [from Will], and from a thousandth part of the power of knowledge, the power of action (kriyā-śakti) arises," it follows that Will alone is the cause of both knowledge and action. Therefore, when the causal Will-power is stilled, there is no fault in the fact that the effectual powers of knowledge and action are also stilled.
Therefore, it has been stated that the state of desire is logically nothing but the absence of knowledge and action.

If it is asked, "In the absence of knowledge, how can there be the activity of desire?", the answer is: true. Knowledge gives rise to desire and action; desire gives rise to knowledge and action; and action gives rise to knowledge and desire. Thus, these three powers are mutually inclusive.

This is indeed the view accepted by all the scriptures (*sakalāgama*). Nevertheless, because it is stated that the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) are included within the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), whose nature consists of existence (*sat*), bliss (*ānanda*), and consciousness (*jñāna*), the power of will alone is first generated due to the proximity of the Supreme Power, whose essential nature is indivisible consciousness.

It is appropriate [to state] that when the mind, which is of the nature of the power of desire (*icchā-śakti*), becomes tranquil, there is the tranquility of all objects of knowledge; thus it has been said. At the end of the *unmanī* state is *paraśiva*. Let us now follow the subject at hand: within the previously established fourfold power, in the group of four powers known as *samana* and *unmanā*, which pervade all powers, resides *anāhataśiva*, the essence of Śiva (*śivatattva*).

The agent is the Lord of Causes; this is the remainder [of the statement]. The nature of the twelve *kalās* is now described: when the activities of the mind have subsided, that is the experience of the *kalā* Unmanā. When the activity of the mind arises again for the self whose mental activity had been completely stilled, that is the experience of the *kalā* Samanā. [This occurs] through the various modes of the mind...

In the state of *vyāpāra* (activity), there is the experience of the pervasive *kalā*. At the time of the exertion (*udyoga*) in the utterance of the mantra, due to the presence of *śakti*, there is the experience of the *kalā* of *śakti*. At the time of the commencement of *nāda*, there is the experience of the *kalā* of *nādānta*. In the form of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) at the conclusion of the mantra, there is the resonance of the sound being heard.

At the junction (*sandhāna*), there is the experience of the *kalā* of Sound (*nāda*). At the conclusion of the utterance of the third part of the emission of the Point (*bindu*), there is the experience of the *kalā* of Obstruction (*nirodhinī*).
During the state of the utterance of the upper half of the Point, there is the experience of the *kalā* of the Half-Moon (*ardhacandra*). [Regarding] the *kalā* of Poison (*viṣa*)...
The experience of the *bindu-kalā* occurs at the very moment of reflecting upon the *bindu* uttered above.

Immediately after, upon the utterance of the syllable *ma*, there is the experience of the *viṣa-kalā*; upon the utterance of *ū*, the experience of the *rasa-kalā*; and upon the utterance of *au*, the experience of the *medhā-kalā*. This is the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*).
If it is asked how, beginning with *Unmanā*, each preceding *kalā* gives rise to each succeeding *kalā*, it is said as follows:

*Medhā* is born from Viṣṇu, who is the cause of *Rasa* and the Lord (*Īśvara*) who is the cause of *Brahman*; *Rasa* is born from Viṣṇu, who is the cause of *Rasa*; *Viṣa* is born from Rudra, who is the cause of *Viṣa*; and *Rudra* is the *bīja* (seed) of [the next stage].

The state of being the object of creation (*sṛjyatva*) for the Cause Maheśvara is the Bindu; the state of being the object of creation for the Cause Maheśvara is the Ardhacandra, Nirodhin, Nāda, and Nādānta;
the state of being the object of creation for the Lord of Causes, Sadāśiva, is the Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.

O Lord of Causes, the fact that the unstruck (anāhata) Śiva is the creator of all beings is established by all the Āgamas; thus, there is no fault in the principle that each subsequent [deity] is the creation of each preceding one.
Now, the method of dissolution (layaprakāra) is written:
the Kuṇḍalinī power residing in the Mūlādhāra; her recitation consists of the mantra whose nature is will (icchā);
the seed-syllable of Śiva, the letter *ha*, which is of the nature of vital breath (*prāṇa*), exists in the form of the letter *ha* as far as the navel-lotus.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*): Subsequently, through the conjunction with *medhā*, there is pervasion up to the heart-lotus by way of the sound *hau*.

At the time of the latter half of the utterance of the *bindu*, there is the pervasion of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). At the moment of the conclusion of the *bindu*, there is the pervasion of *nirodhinī*. Thus, from *medhā* up to *nirodhinī*, [the subtle breath] has arisen from the *mūlādhāra*.

The *nāda* of the letter *ha* is conceived by the practitioner of mantra-repetition as being joined with its *kalā*. Subsequently, the *nāda* becomes subtle and is to be self-realized (*svasaṃvedya*). Its dissolution occurs in the region of the *brahmarandhra*, the location of the end of sound (*nādānta*), above the *nirodhinī*. Immediately after the dissolution of the *nāda*, the *kalā* of the end of sound merges into the *kalā* of its own causal power (*śakti*).

It becomes dissolved. The *kalā* of Śakti dissolves into the *kalā* of Vyāpinī; the *kalā* of Vyāpinī dissolves into the *kalā* of Samanā; and the *kalā* of Samanā also dissolves into the *kalā* of Unmanā. The experience of the *kalā* of Unmanā is now described: having transcended the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth, there arises at that moment a desire.
Having reached the supreme state ending with Śiva through knowledge and action, and having himself become the Supreme Form,
when he remains— having abandoned desire, knowledge, and action, and having realized union with the Supreme— he then becomes the Unmanā state, the experience of the Kalās.
At that time, there is the direct realization of Paraśiva, whose very nature is supreme bliss.
Let us return to the subject at hand. Thus concludes the description of the twelve digits (kalās).

He who does not find the temple endowed with sixteen parts (dviraṣṭaka-kalā) is neither a mantra-practitioner nor a teacher; he merely undergoes fruitless hardship, according to the statement regarding the nature of ritual action. Thus, the temple of sixteen parts is also demonstrated: it extends above the pervasive part (vyāpinī-kalā) and below the part of the Equal One (samanā-kalā).
"Having the form of space, infinite, without protector, and without support"—through this conceptualization of the four parts (*kalā*), there are sixteen parts.
These [parts] extend up to Vyāpinī and Samanā; they are designated as "space-going" and "infinite."
For it is stated that Śiva is endowed with the two [qualities] of being without protector and without support, and possesses sixteen kalās.

Now, based on the statement, "The divisions of *samaya* are five, and those of *viśeṣa* are eight," the two temples consisting of five and eight *kalās* are described. Among them, the one with five *kalās* is as follows, according to the *Siddhāntarahasya*:
"The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*."
"The *hakāra-siddhi* is said to be the fivefold group of phonemes (*kalā-pañcaka*).
The letter *au*, together with the six ending in *bh*, the *bindu*, the half-circle (*vṛttārddha*), the *nāda*,
and joined with *Śakti* and *Samanā*, is indeed Śiva, consisting of eight *kalās*."
Here too, the corruption resulting from the euphonic combination with the letter *ha* is to be inferred.
Thus is the temple consisting of eight parts.
Now, the descriptions concerning the states (*avasthā*) of the temple, such as its utterance (*uccāraṇa*), are written here:
The states are as follows: the waking state is the utterance of the seed-syllable (*bīja*); dreaming is the grasping of the drop (*bindu*);
deep sleep arises from the union with the resonance (*nāda*); and the fourth state (*turya*) would be the gathering of power (*śakti*).
"The state of dissolution within the Fourth (turya) is proclaimed as the supreme abode. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the definition of utterance (uccāraṇa):
having known the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, one should perform the ritual action as desired.

The gross is said to be sound; the subtle consists of thought; that which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the supreme. Thus, there is a threefold utterance according to the divisions of Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava.

That which is appropriate for the utterance [of mantras] presided over by the lords of the meditative states (dhyānasthānādhipati) is the individual (āṇava); that which arises from mere thought is the empowered (śākta); and that which arises from the recollection of Śakti is the Śāmbhava, O Lord of the Assembly of Consciousness.
One should know that the three types—physical, psychosomatic, and supernatural—are the gross form characterized by color and shape;

the subtle is said to be its sound. That which pertains to the one who identifies with the phoneme (varṇābhimānin) is proclaimed as the supreme. Through the methods of *prastāra*, *vistāra*, *tāna*, and *anusandhāna*, he describes the five states. Herein...
*Prastāra* is the drawing of the digits (*kalā*) in the form of a triangle, a plow, a trident, and so forth.
Now, as for the expansion:

the expansion consists of the abode (dhāman), the linga, the body (aṅga), the image (bera), and so forth, within the seven wombs (yoni) and the six paths (adhvan); it exists both in the material realm (ādhibhautika) and in the spiritual realm (ādhyātmika). This is the view of Manu.

The completion of the mantras is established by the statement: "By way of three, five, eight, and twelve *kalās*, there are four [syllables] consisting of short, long, and protracted [vowels], which follow in sequence.
Furthermore: "There is neither sleep nor the dream of consciousness, nor sounds and so forth, nor waking."
"That supreme object of knowledge is pure consciousness alone, devoid of both rejection and acceptance"—
this is the contemplation. Below, the states of stillness and the activity of the two— the mind and the eyes— are indeed declared to be the moon and the sun.
When the moon and sun have perished, this supreme sacrifice brings about all accomplishments.
The five stages beginning with utterance (*uccāraṇa*) are as follows:
the gross movement of sound becomes the *bindu*, the *bindu* also becomes the nature of *nāda*, and *nāda* likewise reaches the state of *śakti*.
Through the process of dissolution (*anulaya*), *śakti* reaches the plane of consciousness (*citpadam*); yet that dissolution does not occur by mere grace (*prasāda*).
Now, the channel of the self-mantra.
Now, the sevenfold state of aesthetic fusion (*samarasa*) pertaining to the principles known as Ātman, Mantreśa, Nāḍī, Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā is as follows:
First, the mantra should be understood as being in a state of aesthetic fusion within the Self; secondly—
The third is known as Nāḍī, followed by Śakti as the fourth;
the fifth is in the location of Vyāpinī, while the sixth is the abode of Samanā.
O Goddess, the seventh [stage], which is the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within reality (*tattva*), is prescribed;
it is to be grasped from the self of the disciple according to the path of the previously mentioned ritual procedure.
Afterwards, having worshipped within oneself, one should contemplate [the deity] as having become liquefied;
[namely] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself.
Therefore, one should utter the Nāda until it has reached dissolution within Śakti;
once the Nāda has entered the center of Śakti, it is then brought forth by means of Śakti.
Therein, consisting of all powers, there arises the state of universal equilibrium;
beyond that, the pervasive [power] and the pervaded attain identity with everything.
Having reached Samanā above that, one should again attain identity with it;
pervading the entire path, one remains established in equanimity.
Wherever the mind goes, one should contemplate the object of knowledge right there;
thus is "equal flavor" (samarasa) described—now learn of the "equinox" (viṣuva).
Now, the characteristics of the seven equinoxes, known as *prāṇa*, *mantra*, *nāḍī*, *praśānta*, *śakti*, *kāla*, and *manaḥ*, are as follows:
*prāṇa*, *mantra*, then *nāḍī*, *praśānta*, and *śakti* as well.
Time, death, and poison—these are said to be its divisions.
Having joined the self and the mind with the vital breath, one becomes equanimous;
one should recite the mantra as long as the mind does not become distracted by anything else.
Situated in the midst of all the channels (nāḍīs),
the one known as Suṣumnā has reached Śiva through the power of the channels.
There, one should cause the nāda to flow; this is called the nāḍī-viṣuva.
The mind should be known as perfectly tranquil, with the range of the senses stilled.
When [the mind] is completely stilled, it should be known as motionless, with mindfulness unmoving;
it is established at the end of the breath within the sixteen *tuṭis*.
Having thus divided the time into three parts for the movement of the vital breath, one should then release it;
the other [breath] is situated at the head of Śakti, while the second is within Vyāpinī.
The third, Samanā, is said to be the equinox (viṣuva) at the place of Sthāna;
beyond that is the goddess Unmanā, wherein one should unite with the Self.
When the self is joined to that, it indeed becomes identical with it;
having understood the equinox according to the rule, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Thus, this commentary on the *Prāsāda-ṣaṭślokī* has been written by me;
having reflected upon it thoroughly, what wise person would not be liberated from bondage?
[Thus ends the commentary on the six verses.]

Because the world consists of females, males, neuters, and so forth, and because its effects are observed, there must be a creator; therefore, the Lord Hara, having first created this [world], brings it forth from himself. || 1 ||
There is no other creator who pervades all; he alone acts according to the karma of beings, performing their creation and dissolution by means of his unified command.
The soul is led away from me by the excess of the mind; it returns through skill and awakening.
Sleep arises from the absence of experience, while awakening exists within the body due to the presence of the atom (the soul) as the knower.
The Self is distinct from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as well as from other [principles], like a minister and a king;
its five states have their own vision and activity obstructed by impurity (mala).
The sense organs perceive objects for the person, but not by themselves; nor does that person [perceive] without Śambhu.
If Śiva were not the one who undergoes transformation through them, he would not lead [the soul] as long as it exists.
If it were invisible, it would be non-existent; if it were visible, it would be insentient.
Therefore, the wise know that the nature of the Knowable is distinct from both Śambhu [the Seer] and those two.

It is not that consciousness is not present in proximity to the conscious, but rather that you two do not know one another; he who knows both the phenomenal world and Śiva is the Self, which is distinct from those two.
Having remained with the senses and the hunters, he was awakened by the thought, "You do not know [the Self].
By means of this power, another fortunate disciple, through the Guru, attains that state.
Having perceived the mirage-like mental fluctuations within the Self that is the witness of consciousness,
and having attained the state of Śiva, the wise one should meditate upon the five-syllabled mantra.
O Siddha, having attained oneness with Śiva, you become dependent upon Him through your own activity; untouched by impurity, māyā, and the like, you exist as pure self-experience alone.
Whether the Self is perceived through vision or through the faculty of hearing, Śiva is its revealer;
therefore, one should cultivate supreme devotion toward Him, who bestows benefit upon the Self.
Having attained those [liberated ones], one should spend a year in the abode of Śiva;
thus is the determination of the meaning of Śaivism for the awakening of knowledge regarding Śiva. || 12 ||
The *Śivajñānabodhasūtra* declares that the Prāsāda [mantra] is fivefold; its divisions shall be explained in sequence:
the Pure Root, the Tattva, the Ādi, and the Ātman—thus it is fivefold.
Śuddha Haṃ. Mūla Hrauṃ. Tatva Haṃ. Ādi Hauṃ. Ātmā Haṃsaḥ.

Homage!
The root mantra is not used at all for the invocation; rather, each respective *brahma-ṣaḍaṅga* mantra is used.
The water for the feet (*pādya*) is offered with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the *vāmadeva* mantra.

homage to Sadyojāta. || 5 ||
The six-limbed [mantra]:

"Salutation to Sadyojāta," [with this] water for the feet; "Salutation to Vāmadeva," [with this] water for sipping; "Salutation to Aghora," [with this] clothing; "Salutation to Tatpuruṣa," [with this] ornaments; "Salutation to Īśāna," "Salutation to the Heart," [with this] perfume;
"Salutation to the Head," flowers; "Salutation to the Crest," incense; "Salutation to the Armor," [with this] the armor.
Homage to the lamp; homage to the three eyes for the *ārātrika* rite; homage to the weapon-mantra for the flower on the face.
May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the teacher Subrahmaṇya.
Invocation, installation, presence, confinement, facing [the deity], and veiling.
And when he is well-pleased and bestows boons, these are proclaimed as the eight mudrās.
Salutations to Śambhu, who has become the immovable pillar (Sthāṇu), whose self is enveloped by the light of the liṅga,
and whose limbs are illuminated by the shadow of his fourfold form.
The sound-mantra is "Śiva-śivacaraṇa-śivānanda-śiva śivāya namaḥ."
The mantra for the palace.
The Prāsāda mantra was taught by Śiva to the illustrious Guru Skanda as follows:

*prāṇa*, *medhā*, and that which is called *kṣamā*; above that, *garala* and *cetana*; the half-lotus (*ardhābja*) and the upward-pointing [triangle] (*ūrdhva*); then the staff (*daṇḍa*), and beyond that, the lower power (*aparā-śakti*) should be known; at the end of *unmanā*, Śiva is to be expressed, and likewise the portion consisting of Power (*śakti-kala*).
The moon and likewise the sun are thus [the lords of the hours].
It is said "of the Guru" either because Subrahmaṇya is also a Guru among Gurus, or because Agastya and others are Gurus;
by this qualification of Subrahmaṇya as a Guru, it is indicated that the grace and application belong only to Gurus and not to others.

The meaning is that Śiva, by means of the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, has taught the *prāsāda* [mantra] according to its phonemes as his own preferred [form]. Here, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *prāsāda* is stated in the *Śuddhākhyā*: "The syllable *prā* signifies the knowledge of Śiva, and the syllable *sā* is said to be 'going' (*gati*)."
The nature of the ten syllables is what is designated as the temple (prāsāda).
Because it bestows liberation through knowledge, it is therefore called *prāsāda*;
there is no Śiva higher than knowledge, nor is there anything equal to it.
This is proclaimed as the supreme knowledge and as the temple (prāsāda).
The characteristic of the temple is stated thus with three and a half powers:
one should join the sixth [vowel] to the end of the thirteenth [consonant] within the fifth [vowel].
One should know Śiva-tantu to be the mantra-form within Sadāśiva.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The temple (prāsāda), joined with the sixth [vowel], and again joined at the end of the sixth [vowel], conjoined with Śiva and Śakti—this is called here the root mantra. Thus it is said.
He demonstrates that very point here with the words "yathā" and so forth: *prāṇahara* (the life-taker) is the vowel *au*; *medhā* (intellect) is the vowel *ū*;
above that, further up, is *garala* (poison), which is the syllable *ma*; and *cetanā* (consciousness) is the *bindu*. Thus is the three-part mantra.
The sky is crooked, empty, the ether, illusion, Śiva-nature, the firmament, and Lakṣmī—this is the pentad.
The resonance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is expressed by the syllable *ha* through the word "vital breath.
The vowel *au* marks the end of the vision, and likewise, there is the one beyond the chief *ulkā*.
The Anvāhārya oblation is Caru, Medhā, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Janārdana.
By the word *medhā*, the vowel *au* is expressed;
and the fifth, *cetanā*, is said to be the head of *sumanā*, according to the rule.
By the word *cetanā*, the *bindu* (drop) is expressed; thus it should be understood through the sequence of synonyms, beginning with *mā*.

Because it consists of nine aspects, the number nine is indicated. Śiva, joined with those numbers [of phonemes] beginning with *kalā*, is the signified (*vācya*) in the manner described; the sense is that "Śiva is *kala*. Thus, the scripture states:
"The end of *sa*, *medhā* (the letter *ma*), the sixth [consonant] (*ṭa*), the end of *bha* (*ba*), along with the *bindu*, the half-moon, and the *nāda*."
"Sound (nāda) is that [state], the power (śakti) moving above it is unmanā, and the undivided is Śiva.

According to this manner which is about to be described, Śiva—the temple of sixteen digits, who is the digit of the moon—is the signified; likewise, according to the manner about to be described, Śiva—the temple of twelve digits, who is the digit of the sun—is also the signified.
This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). Due to the divisions of twenty, sixteen, twelve, ten, nine, eight, six, and five *kalās*, the temple (*prāsāda*) is of eight kinds.
One should always mutter the Śiva-mantra; thus, within the midst of these eight kinds of temples, [it is situated].
The three palaces presented are the Sakala, Niṣkala, and Śūnya; the Khalaḍhya is adorned with a lotus.
Kṣapaṇa is situated within Kṣamayantī, and Kaṇṭheṣya is remembered as the eighth.

First, the face of this [deity] is proclaimed as Raudrī on the left; Ambikā is said to be the multitude [of teeth]; Jyeṣṭhā resides at the tips of the nails.
Icchā is situated in the region of the head, and Kriyā is located below that.

The Knower [perceives] the form of the Mother of Letters (Varṇāmbikā) through the word "Gaṇeśa," which consists of four quarters and is composed of the mantra that is half of half of the letter *Ī*. Thus, the unmanifest form of the Mother of Letters, whose nature is the sound of resonance (*dhvani*), is established as consisting of eleven parts and being composed of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*). One should perceive that...
The meaning is that he pays homage to the *siddhamātṛkā*, the mother of the Rudras beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.

It is said that even a man rivals the Sun, Tārkṣya, the Moon, Kandarpa, Śaṅkara, Anala, and Viṣṇu (sc) because he possesses qualities such as attracting [others] like them. Thus it is stated: "even a man."
Since even a single syllable or a single mora of this [mantra] is thus renowned for its greatness— namely,

that it is the "bonding of the digits" which brings about tranquility— the meaning is that its very nature is the accomplishment of peace. The intended sense is that it destroys [suffering] and delivers its own devotees from the jaws of death.

With the third sūtra, beginning with "yadakṣare" and ending with "viṣṇubhiḥ," he demonstrates the intermediate fruit for one who meditates on the sequence of phonemes by way of contrast (vyatireka). Here, the imperishable (*akṣara*) to be attained is the letter *sa*;
it is situated within the second and third [sections], extending from the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*) up to the shell of the universe (*kaṭāha*), and from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) onwards.
The three [syllables] above that, ending with Śiva, are qualifiers. In this sūtra also, the majesty of the letter *ha* contained within the Root-Vidyā should be understood as indicated.

In this context, according to the *Akṣaramahāpadāsūtra*, the letter *ha* is considered to be the indicator of the universe (*viśvasūcika*). And that letter *ha* is seen as being followed by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the manner of the *mātṛkā*; thus, the letter *e*, which occupies the eleventh position in the numbering of the *mātṛkā* and consists of a triangle, belongs to this Supreme Deity.

In both the external and internal divisions, there is the "seating" by means of the seed-syllable of the support; this is explained in each quarter [of the verse]. That which is the single [unit] situated in the eleven locations, being triangular in nature, is itself the syllable *ī*; it becomes the form of the letter *ī*.
This is the meaning of its "state of abiding. Furthermore, even at the time of abiding, it reaches a state fit for perception, and those two constitute the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*).

In its individualized form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpeṇa*), O auspicious one, the disciple and the teacher [enter] into the state of the liberator from bonds for the sake of the disciple’s body; this is the meaning. The letters beginning with *varṇa* and so forth, though manifest, are not counted separately because they are produced by the conjunction of the forms of the vowels *a*, *ka*, *ra*, and *kṣa*. Furthermore, the letter *la* is also not [counted separately] because it is included within the letter *la*.

A separate enumeration: thus, when the *makāras* are established in the manner described, they are understood to consist of sixty-seven [units]. As it has been said regarding Gaṇeśa: he takes that syllable *ha*; *graha* is the mental syllable *sa*; and in the word *nakṣatra*, there are the syllables *na* and *ṣa*.

The syllable *kāra* has the sense of "making. Here, however, only the syllable *bra* is taken as the imperishable (*akṣara*) Brahman. In the word *nakṣatre*, the syllable *na* is [the first part] and *kṣa* is *yoginī*. By the term *yoginī*, the *piṇḍi* (the aggregate) is meant, which is the syllable *ha*. In the word *rūpī*, the syllables *u* and *pa* are for the purpose of pronunciation; only the letter *ra* is taken. In the word *ṇī*, the syllable *ṇa* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

Only the vowel *ī* is taken. Combining all of this results in the first [syllable]. Here, in the word *nakṣatra*, the letters *na* and *ka* are for the purpose of pronunciation; the letter *k* is adopted according to the rule of "half-omission" (*ardhalopa*). Here, as before, the Supreme Lord is the letter *ha*, and the Yoginī is the form of the zodiac sign (*rāśi*). In this verse, the vowel *ī*...
Regarding the statement that there are four [parts], the third begins with the word *gaṇeśa* and so forth; by this alone, the mantra becomes complete through three repetitions.
This is stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "Then there are those called Prāṇa, Medhā, and Kṣamā, followed by Garala."

Above the lotus of volition (*cetanā*), there should be a staff (*daṇḍa*); for one who moves, another power (*śakti*) is to be known at the end of *unmanā*. Śiva is to be expressed as the portion (*kala*) of Speech-power (*vāk-śakti*), and likewise the portion of the Moon; [these are] the two at the beginning. The Self (*ātman*) is *haṃsa*; the principle (*tattva*) is *haṃ*; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the letter *ha*; and intelligence (*medhā*) is the vowel *au*.
Kṣamā is the letter Ū; Śuddha is HA; Mūla is HARUṂ;
Lakāra is Śivamā, as well as Puran and Āda;
the seed-syllable of Vidyā is KṢA, and it is indeed the final letter of the kūṭas.
The letter *sa*, which is the final of its class (*vargānta*), is the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) in the form of the *bindu*.
*Nāda* is held to be its beginning. The letter *la* is the subtle *nāda*;
in the western [direction] it is the subtle *nāda*, while in the northern [direction] it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vidyā.
The seed-syllable of the Vidyā is *kṣaṃ*; it is said that the vowels are long.
The *pluta* vowel is to be known as having three morae (*mātrā*); a long vowel (*ajina*) consists of one and a half morae;
and a short vowel consists of half a mora—these are said to be the definitions.
The syllable *au* is to be known as the earth; *na* is said to be the wind.
Likewise, *ū* is the upward vital breath (*prāṇa*), and *ka* is the vital breath that is the moon.
The Equinox.
Desiring to experience the sport of uprooting the tree of obstacles,
I salute the Leader of the Gaṇas as he plays in the guise of an elephant.
First, the breath-equinox (prāṇa-viṣuva) is to be known as the mantra;
second is the channel-equinox (nāḍi-viṣuva); and the fourth is the state of perfect tranquility (praśānta).
The fifth is the Śakti-viṣuva; the sixth is called Kevala;
the seventh is the Anta-viṣuva, which is said to be its division.

In the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*, the path taught by the Guru consists of the recitation of mantras preceded by the contemplation of the practice of the equinox (*viṣuva*) according to the method instructed by the Guru. And this equinox is sevenfold for the Teacher, through the peaceful vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) that has entered into the beginning and the end.

The union of the disciple’s superior mind with [the breath] is first called the "equinox of the vital breath" (prāṇaviṣuva). Having joined the mind of the self with the vital breaths, it becomes the equinox;
having meditated upon the dissolution of the self through its own resonance (nāda) in the locations beginning with the heart, [one proceeds] with the letters beginning with *ha*.
The contemplation of the mantra is distinguished by the sequential pronunciation of the conjunctions of the name-mantras;
that which is designated as the "equinox" (viṣuva) consists of the mantras from the heart up to the point of the bindu.

The second [practice] is the contemplation upon the piercing of the knots located within the *suṣumnā*, known as the penis, the *kandarpa*, the navel, the heart, the pericarp, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), and the limit of twelve fingers (*dvādaśānta*).
The third is the equinox (*viṣuva*) from the heart up to the point of the *bindu*; it is to be contemplated by means of the root trident (*mūla-triśūla*) within the causal principles (*kāraṇa*).

By abandoning the six positions—Ha, O, Ma, Bindu, Nāda, and Anta—within Brahmā and the others, there is the Nāda in the place of Śakti; this is the fourth, the Tranquil Equinox (praśānta-viṣuva). When the Nāda situated in the middle of Śakti moves upward as it were, that is the fifth, the Śakti Equinox (śakti-viṣuva).

The sixth is the *viṣuva* of time, which consists of the hundredfold immeasurable power of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), of all the winds, and even of every internal portion; it is pervaded by the power of the principle of life (*jīva-tattva*) and is known as *samanā*.
Devoid even of that sixth [state] in the form of *unmanī*, at its conclusion is the mantra of the grace of Supreme Śiva.
The consciousness of the disciple, along with the dissolution, is [withdrawn] through the sound of abandonment (*tyāga*) at the end of the objects of the sense of taste;
the first void occurs at the cessation of the *bindu*, the half-moon, and the *nirodhinī*, while the second void occurs at the cessation of the *nāda*, the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*), and *śakti*.
